units.text: Begin with compute and memory. Compute-optimized families suit CPU-heavy processing, while memory-optimized families suit large working sets and caches. Choose from the workload's measured bottleneck rather than the family letter alone.

Compare general purpose with storage optimized. General purpose balances CPU and memory for many application tiers. Storage-optimized instances target high local input and output, but local disks still need an explicit durability plan.

Look at accelerated and burstable computing. GPU workloads need a compatible accelerator and software stack. Burstable instances address variable CPU demand with a baseline and credits; sustained demand can change performance or cost.

With the full slide visible, validate the whole instance. Check virtual CPUs, memory, processor architecture, EBS bandwidth, network throughput and packet rate. Benchmark representative traffic before committing to a family and size.
Start with the CPU-credit illustration. Credits accumulate when CPU use is below baseline and are spent above it. Standard mode becomes constrained when the available credit balance is exhausted.

Stay with the lower credit panels and compare Unlimited mode. Sustained surplus-credit use can add charges. Monitor credit balance and sustained CPU demand, rather than judging the instance from a single brief spike.

Move to the Arm64 and software panels. Graviton requires a compatible Arm64 image and supported operating system; Windows is not supported. Check application binaries, container images, native libraries, agents and commercial software.

With the whole slide restored, separate the two decisions. Bursting is CPU accounting; Graviton is processor architecture. Benchmark compatible options for latency, throughput and total cost instead of assuming either label guarantees a better result.
Start with reboot. Restarting the guest operating system clears volatile runtime state, while EBS and instance-store data normally remain. A reboot is not the same operation as stopping the instance.
Move to stop and start. EBS volumes persist, but RAM and instance-store data are lost. The underlying host can change, so important data must not depend on those temporary local resources.

Inspect hibernation. On supported configurations, RAM is saved to an encrypted EBS root volume and restored when the instance resumes. Check the prerequisites and storage capacity; instance-store data still does not survive.

With the full slide visible, compare termination. The instance is permanently removed, and EBS retention depends on delete-on-termination settings. Design backups and retention deliberately, using the lifecycle operation that matches the workload.
